drills.q: List the nine sections of the design-doc template in order.
drills.a: Context and constraints; requirements including NON-GOALS; architecture plus decomposition criterion; key decisions (chose X over Y because Z, accepted cost C); data model; scale numbers; failure modes symptom-first; what I would change now; hardest questions with answers.

drills.q: How many boxes in an interview diagram, and how long to narrate it?
drills.a: At most nine boxes, 90 seconds, left-to-right data flow, drill-down target in the middle. More than nine and you have drawn deployment topology instead of architecture.

drills.q: Compute the vector payload for 1.2M rows at 512 dimensions, float32, and say what it implies.
drills.a: 1.2M x 512 x 4 bytes = ~2.5 GB. It fits in memory on a single node, so a distributed vector store buys capacity you do not need, which is the first argument for indexing in place.

drills.q: 'Why not a real vector database?' Give the three reasons in priority order.
drills.a: 1) Every query is filtered by tenant and locale; colocating vectors with relational columns makes the filter a native predicate with granule pruning rather than a metadata filter on an ANN index. 2) ~2.5 GB fits in memory on one node. 3) One fewer system to keep consistent, backfill and page on. Plus a documented migration trigger: ~10x rows, a second consumer, or a hard hybrid-search requirement.

drills.q: Retrieval latency grows superlinearly as tenants are added. Diagnose it.
drills.a: tenant_id is not a prefix of the ClickHouse ordering key, so the tenant filter cannot prune granules and the query degrades to post-filtering, over-fetching by the inverse of the selectivity. It is a table-definition problem, not an ANN tuning problem.

drills.q: A tenant has only 50 skill items. Is the shared HNSW index the right retrieval path?
drills.a: No. Below a few thousand vectors an exact scan is both faster and exact, and HNSW graph connectivity degrades at small cardinality. The retrieval path should choose by tenant cardinality. A shared index with a tenant filter is still better for small tenants than a per-tenant index would be, but exact search is better still.

drills.q: Derive peak rps and the uncached downstream call rate for the recommendation platform.
drills.a: 2M users, 10% DAU = 200K; 5 views each = 1M requests/day; /86,400 = ~12 rps average; 5-10x peak = 60-120 rps. At 100+ content IDs hydrated per request, uncached that is 6,000-12,000 downstream calls/sec, which is why the cache is load-bearing rather than an optimisation.

drills.q: 'Why eight services? Convince me it wasn't resume-driven architecture.'
drills.a: Criterion: independent scaling and independent failure, not tidy entities. Three profiles diverge: latency-bound serving, throughput-bound ingestion, batch profile processing. Colocating means provisioning for the worst and letting a batch run take down serving. Then concede: eight is more than the criterion justifies, at least two would be merged today because they always changed and deployed together, and the cost was continuous (eight pipelines, eight dashboard sets, distributed tracing for one user question).

drills.q: A hot cache key expires and every replica stampedes the external API. Fix it.
drills.a: Jittered TTLs so keys do not expire in lockstep; single-flight or a short per-key lock so one fetch populates all waiters; stale-while-revalidate so waiters get the old value while one refreshes. Jitter alone is partial: the herd is a concurrency problem, not just a scheduling one.

drills.q: State precisely what MCP gives you that a shared library does not, and the cost.
drills.a: Versioned contracts and consumer independence: a library couples every consumer to your release cycle, language and runtime, so a breaking change is a coordinated upgrade across every importer. Cost: a network hop and serialisation per tool call, plus operating the servers. Wrong choice for a latency-critical inner loop; right for a pipeline measured in seconds per item.

drills.q: 'Most multi-agent systems are one agent with extra latency.' Respond, then name a merge candidate.
drills.a: State the test: separate agents only when failure modes, scaling profiles or deploy cadences genuinely differ. Transcript processing fails on malformed input, chunking fails by producing bad boundaries (a quality failure, not an error), gap detection fails by producing unaccepted findings; three different on-call responses and rollback decisions. Merge candidate: transcript processing and contextual chunking, which always run in sequence on the same input. Keep gap detection separate: different trigger and cadence.

drills.q: Three sequential agent steps at 95% each. End-to-end success? At ten steps and 85%?
drills.a: 0.95^3 = ~86%, so roughly one in seven runs fails somewhere. 0.85^10 = ~20%. This is the argument for checkpointing rather than retry tuning: checkpointing removes the multiplication by making the failed step the only work redone.

drills.q: What limits concurrency on a vLLM endpoint? Derive it for an 8B fp16 model on a 24 GB GPU.
drills.a: KV cache, not FLOPs. ~16 GB of weights leaves ~6-7 GB after framework overhead. KV per token is roughly 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x 2 bytes, order 100-200 KB/token for an 8B-class config, so ~30,000-60,000 tokens of aggregate context, i.e. roughly 15-30 concurrent sequences at 2,000 tokens. Present it as an order-of-magnitude derivation with assumptions named.

drills.q: GPU utilisation is 40% and inference is slow. What is wrong and what is the wrong move?
drills.a: KV cache exhaustion: the GPU is idle because it cannot admit more sequences, so requests wait for cache blocks. Fixes: reduce max sequence length, reduce max concurrent sequences, or add GPU memory. The wrong move is reading 40% as spare capacity and adding traffic.

drills.q: Why Bedrock batch offline and self-hosted vLLM online? Defend running two providers.
drills.a: Different workload shapes: online is latency-bound with concurrent short requests and wants owned capacity plus continuous batching; offline is throughput-bound with nothing waiting and wants the cheapest per-token option with NO capacity coupling to serving. Pushing a 1M-row job through the real-time endpoint is how a scheduled job becomes a latency incident. Two providers is only worth it when offline volume is large enough to move online p99; below that, one path with a priority queue is simpler.

drills.q: Your PySpark job calls an LLM from 20 executors. How do you avoid rate limiting, and what is the classic trap?
drills.a: Bound in-flight concurrency rather than relying on retry, because a rate limit is a throughput ceiling and retrying into it amplifies load. Trap: a per-executor budget multiplies by executor count, so 20 executors at 10 in flight is 200. A global budget requires a shared counter (a distributed rate limiter) with its own choice between failing closed (stalls the job) and failing open (recreates the problem). Reducing executor count is the wrong fix: it throttles the whole job for one stage.

drills.q: A batch inference job reports success but downstream data is incomplete. Explain and fix.
drills.a: Batch inference fails PARTIALLY: rows fail on content filtering, malformed input or length limits, and the job completes with fewer output rows. Missing rows look like absent data rather than failed processing, so it is silent. Fix: row-count reconciliation between input and output, a failure manifest, and a downstream contract that refuses partial input. Keep row_count and rows_failed in your own job table, not only in provider logs.

drills.q: 'How would you scale this 10x?' Give the four-step shape and apply it to the skill resolution engine.
drills.a: 1) Ask what is scaling: users, data, or requests per user. 2) Name what breaks first and why: the cross-encoder reranker, since it cannot be precomputed and its cost is linear in candidates times QPS. 3) Name the SYMPTOM: p99 growing while error rate stays flat, queue time growing faster than compute. 4) Fix and then what breaks next: cut top-k, batch across requests, consider a distilled cross-encoder; next constraint is index memory, sharded by tenant since tenant is already the query scope.

drills.q: Name the weakest part of each of the five flagship systems.
drills.a: Skills platform: no hybrid lexical stage, so exact matches pay for an embedding model. Recommendation platform: no off-policy evaluation, so every policy change was a live experiment. Agent pipeline: chunk quality is unmeasured and upstream of everything. LLM serving: no dollar cost model / break-even. Query Crafter: correctness was never measured, only adoption.

drills.q: 'You have described a lot of AI systems. Convince me you can do plain backend engineering.'
drills.a: Reach for the non-AI material: atomic concurrent updates on MongoDB, async client lifecycle under multi-worker servers, distributed cache design including thundering-herd handling, multi-tenant object-level authorization, a Java-to-Python migration with a verifiable cutover, an Airflow migration off Jenkins, and a pipeline rebuild from 4.5 hours to 30 minutes. None of that is AI work and all of it is why the AI systems stayed up. Reaching for another AI story after being asked for a non-AI one is the failure.
